---
title: "Prior work"
---

## Summary

This project is not the first to build on UK company data, and it deliberately reuses and
benchmarks against what exists rather than starting from scratch. Investigative teams have used
the PSC and Land Registry data to trace ownership (Global Witness, Private Eye and its
successors, Transparency International UK); open-data organisations maintain standard-format
ownership pipelines (Open Ownership, OpenSanctions); a long-running project links charities to
companies (Find that Charity); and an academic literature studies small-company default and
filing behaviour. Most of these are one-off investigations; a few maintain ongoing pipelines.
The recurring lesson is that the genuine data advantage sits in the private layer none of them
can rebuild — and that open, reproducible infrastructure is where there is still a real gap to
fill.

## Details

Each entry below: what it did, the tools it used, links to the organisation, and what it means
for this project. Source: deck slide 7 and its notes
(`docs/source-material/companies-house-accounts-deck.md`,
`companies-house-accounts-notes.md`) and the literature queue
(`literature/open-company-uk-source-queue-2026-08.md`). **[Checked]** against those files; "most
projects are one-off investigations" is a judgement, not a measurement.

### [Global Witness](https://www.globalwitness.org/) + DataKind UK — "The Companies We Keep" (2018)

- **What:** an early analysis of the PSC register, with public code and open notebooks. Matched
  people using a combination of name, birth month/year, and address.
- **Tools:** graph database, open Jupyter notebooks.
- **For us:** the natural benchmark for this project's [PSC person
  matching](../datasets/psc.qmd) — compare approaches and match confidence directly rather than
  re-deriving a method.

### Private Eye → Who Owns England → [TaxPolicy.org.uk](https://taxpolicy.org.uk/) (2015–2026)

- **What:** a line of work mapping offshore ownership of UK property from Land Registry data. The
  2026 map cross-checks the **overseas-entities register** against Land Registry records and
  **publishes its method**.
- **For us:** reuse the Land-Registry-to-overseas-entity method when the [Land Registry
  source](../guide/sources-map.qmd#hm-land-registry-company-property-ownership) is integrated,
  rather than reinventing the join.

### Transparency International UK — "Track and Trace", "Behind the Masks"

- **What:** analysis of Covid-era public contracts; found **£15.3bn** of high-risk contracts, with
  red flags including suppliers that were only **weeks old** (using incorporation dates).
- **For us:** company age is a usable register signal. The repository already has a
  **`YOUNG_COMPANY`** flag (age < 24 months) — but it is deliberately **`info`** severity, context
  only, and never counts toward any total, consistent with this project's no-composite-score
  line. Source: the generated [rule
  reference](https://github.com/ThomasHSimm/open-company-uk/blob/main/docs/rules.md). (The deck
  slide suggested adding a company-age flag; this corrects it — one already exists, as context.)

### [Open Ownership](https://www.openownership.org/) + [OpenSanctions](https://www.opensanctions.org/)

- **What:** open pipelines that convert UK PSC data into standard formats — Open Ownership's
  `bods-uk-psc-pipeline` (Beneficial Ownership Data Standard) and OpenSanctions' `gb-coh-psc`
  (now part of `opensanctions/graph`, FollowTheMoney format). Open Ownership has combined its
  output with procurement (Open Contracting) and sanctions data. A closely related applied study
  is Jofre & Knobel (2025), [*Insights from the United Kingdom's People with Significant Control
  register*](https://www.openownership.org/en/publications/insights-from-the-united-kingdoms-people-with-significant-control-register/).
- **For us:** reuse these PSC pipelines and the standard formats; add sanctions links. These are
  maintained pipelines, not one-off investigations — the model to follow for the [PSC
  work](../datasets/psc.qmd).

### David Kane / 360Giving — [Find that Charity](https://findthatcharity.uk/)

- **What:** links **16 sources and ~660,000 non-profits**; many charities are also companies and
  carry a company number. The same author wrote **`ixbrlparse`**, the library this project
  benchmarks its [accounts parser](../datasets/accounts-validation.qmd) against.
- **For us:** charity lookup is already solved — reuse Find that Charity rather than building a
  [charity join](../guide/sources-map.qmd#charity-registers-charity-commission-oscr-ccni).

### Academic research

- **What:** a systematic review of **145 studies** on predicting small-company default found
  nearly half used commercial data services. A 2024 study of **8,490 UK charitable companies**
  found they file later when in financial difficulty (see also Clatworthy & Peel 2016 on
  private-company filing timeliness, in the [evidence register](register.qmd)).
- **For us:** that so much of the default literature leans on *paid* data is exactly the gap an
  open, reproducible dataset can help fill — while being honest that filing behaviour is not, by
  itself, a validated predictor of fraud or insolvency.

### Common tools, and the gap

Across these projects the recurring toolset is Jupyter and pandas, graph databases (Neo4j),
Elasticsearch, linked data (RDF/SPARQL), and DuckDB. **Most projects are one-off investigations**;
Open Ownership and OpenSanctions are the exceptions that maintain pipelines.

> **What it means for this project.** None of this prior work can be rebuilt from Companies House
> alone where it depends on the private data layer (bank data, trade payments, judgments). The gap
> it *can* fill is open, documented, reproducible infrastructure over the free sources — which is
> the positioning of this whole project: explain and connect what exists, publish usable data, and
> add code only where it adds something.
